title: Stop Blaming the AI: How Disciplined Engineering Makes Generative AI Work

SOUNDING BOARD Editor: John Favaro Trust-IT jfavaro@gmail.com Stop Blaming the AI: How Disciplined Engineering Makes Generative AI Work Kurt Antony Richardson Digital Object Identifier 10.1109/MS.2026.3684756 Date of current version: 30 June 2026 A GROWING CHORUS in the tech industry is sounding the alarm: Generative AI is creating a tsunami of technical debt. Developers are prompting their way to fragile, unmaintainable codebases. The phenomenon even has a name: “vibe coding,” coined by AI researcher Andrej Karpathy, who described it as “fully giv[ing] in to the vibes, embrace[ing] exponen - tials, and forget[ting] that the code even exists.”a The critics aren’t wrong about the problem. But they’re catastrophically wrong about the diagnosis. aA. Karpathy, “There’s a new kind of coding I call ‘vibe coding’…” X (formerly Twitter), Feb. 3, 2025. [Online]. Available: https://x.com/karpathy/status/ 1886192184808149383 To be fair, vibe coding has legiti - mate uses. Borg, Bjarnason, and Hedin recently demonstrated that vibe coding can be remarkably effective for rapid prototyping—enabling high-fidelity, executable prototypes that communicate product vision, validate require - ments, and align teams far faster than traditional methods.1 Their research identifies five distinct prototyping purposes—external communica - tion, internal alignment, validation and testing, incremental development, and exploration—where the speed and accessibility of vibe coding deliver genuine value, even for nontechnical practitioners. The danger isn’t vibe coding itself; it’s mistaking a prototyping technique for a production development methodology. Generative AI is remarkably good at writing code. The issue is that many people are using it in ways that virtually guarantee failure—and the solution has been hiding in plain sight for decades. It’s called systems engineering. When you pair disci - plined engineering with generative AI, the results are transformative. The Limitation Nobody Wants to Talk About Before we get to the solution, we need to understand the core techni - cal constraint that makes vibe coding so dangerous for production systems: context dilution. Large language models operate within a finite context window. As that window fills with thousands of lines of existing code, architectural decisions, and the sprawling state of a large application, the model’s abil - ity to reason coherently degrades. From the Editor What is the key to scaling up the impressive capabilities of AI-assisted coding into production quality? To paraphrase a classic film, we've always had the key, we’ve had it all along, says our author Kurt Richardson: It is systems engineering discipline. And this also has important implications for how we should be managing our engineering workforce, he argues.— John Favaro

pages.text: 112 IEEE SOFTWARE | WWW.COMPUTER.ORG/SOFTWARE | @IEEESOFTWARE SOUNDING BOARD It’s a fundamental property of how attention mechanisms work in trans - former architectures. When you ask an LLM to “add user authentication to my app” and that app is already 50,000 lines of interconnected code, you’re asking the model to comprehend a complex system while generating code that integrates cleanly with it. The model doesn’t “understand” the codebase the way an experienced developer does. It’s pattern-matching across a diluted sea of tokens, and output quality degrades proportionally with input complexity. Anyone with a working under - standing of these models would rec - ognize this as a serious constraint for large-scale development. And yet the prevailing approach has been to ignore it—to treat LLMs as omniscient coding oracles. This is not a failure of artificial intelli - gence. It is a failure of engineering judgment. Working With the Grain Here’s what we’ve learned building production systems with generative AI at the core of our development workflow: AI-assisted code genera - tion doesn’t replace engineering discipline—it amplifies whatever discipline you bring. Bring none, and it ampli - fies chaos. Bring rigor, and it ampli - fies productivity in ways difficult to overstate. Our guiding principle is simple: Give the AI well-defined, manage - able problems to solve. That’s the insight separating teams shipping reliable AI-generated code from teams drowning in technical debt. In practice, this means doing something that software engineering has always demanded but that vibe coding explicitly rejects: planning before building. The Process Phase 1: Systems Engineering and Decomposition Before generating code, we invest in upfront systems engineering—iden - tifying core functionality, defining clean interfaces, and decomposing the system into discrete, indepen - dently implementable components. Generative AI excels at supporting this phase: requirements analysis, interface definition, architecture de - composition. These are tasks where LLMs add tremendous value because the context is focused and the output is structured reasoning. The goal is a set of microservices, and we mean “micro.” Each service encapsulates a single coherent func - tion behind a well-defined interface, typically no more than a couple thousand lines—small enough to be fully comprehended within a single, fo - cused AI generation context. This isn’t arbitrary; it’s a direct response to context dilution. Phase 2: Requirements and Implementation Planning With architecture defined, we write software requirements for each mi - croservice and establish a pull re - quest schedule. Each PR is scoped to a manageable increment. AI excels here too—given a well-defined inter - face and clear behavioral intent, an LLM can generate detailed require - ments, identify test cases, and sug - gest implementation sequences with impressive quality. Phase 3: Incremental, Verified Code Generation We have AI generate code for each PR—and we test between each step. This is nonnegotiable. Every incre - ment is verified against requirements before the next begins. This catches errors early and keeps the AI’s con - text clean for each generation step. Phase 4: Composition and Integration Once building blocks are verified, we compose them into full solutions. The microservice architecture means integration is primarily wiring welltested components together. Because each component has a defined inter - face and verified behavior, composi - tion is predictable and debuggable. The productivity payoff is sub - stantial. Solutions that would have taken months can come together in weeks—not because we cut cor - ners, but because AI eliminated the mechanical burden of translating well-understood requirements into working code. Why This Works The reason this approach succeeds where vibe coding often fails is sim - ple alignment: We structure work to match what generative AI is actually good at. Give it a clear specification, fo - cused scope, and bounded problem space, and generated code quality is remarkably high. Give it a vague prompt and a sprawling codebase, and you get what critics rightly com - plain about: brittle, inconsistent code that appears to work until it cata - strophically doesn’t. There is emerging empirical sup - port for this principle. Borg, Bjar - nason, and Hedin 1 observed that a vibe-coded prototype built with the Lovable platform—roughly 6,000 lines of TypeScript produced entirely through conversational prompting— scored 9.6 out of 10 on CodeScene’s CodeHealth maintainability metric. The authors attribute this partly to Lovable’s prompt engineering, which favors highly modular React com - ponents, and partly to the bounded

pages.text: SOUNDING BOARD scope of the project itself. This rein - forces the central point: When the problem space is constrained and the components are modular, AI-gener - ated code quality can be remarkably high. The issue has never been the AI’s coding ability; it’s the size and clarity of the problem you give it. This isn’t novel. Decompose com - plex problems into manageable pieces, define clear interfaces, implement incrementally, verify continuously—these principles have governed effective software development for decades. The tool has changed. The engineer - ing principles haven’t. Humans in the Loop There’s a temptation, even among disciplined teams, to let the process become too automated. This needs to be addressed directly: effective AI-assisted development requires ac - tive human oversight at every phase. During systems engineering, AI can propose architectures that look elegant but contain subtle flaws. A senior engineer isn’t rubber-stamping; they’re applying experiential judg - ment that no model possesses. When the AI gets it wrong, the human guides it: refining prompts, adding constraints, iterating until output re - flects genuine engineering judgment. AI-generated requirements can be impressively comprehensive and simultaneously miss the point—enumer - ating functional requirements while overlooking the one nonfunctional constraint that should have shaped the entire specification. Human review catches gaps that emerge from the model’s lack of situational awareness. The per-PR code generation phase is where human oversight pays its most visible dividends. Each increment needs review not just for functional correctness but for readability, maintainability, and robustness. When code falls short, the engineer guides the AI toward better solutions. This iterative dialogue—not first-pass generation—is where production-grade code emerges. As Simon Willison put it: “If an LLM wrote every line of your code, but you’ve reviewed, tested, and un - derstood it all, that’s not vibe coding in my book—that’s using an LLM as a typing assistant.” b The pattern across all phases is generation, validation, and guided refinement. Teams that skip this loop accumu - late the technical debt the industry is rightly worried about. The Talent Pipeline Crisis While the industry debates AIgenerated code quality, quieter and arguably more consequential decisions are being made in hiring departments globally. Companies are simultane - ously slashing junior engineering headcount and pushing experienced engineers toward the exits. Both moves are driven by the same flawed logic. The junior hiring freeze is the more visible trend. According to SignalFire, entry-level hiring at major tech firms has dropped more than 50% over the past three years. c A Stanford Digital Economy Study found that employ - ment for software developers aged 22–25 declined nearly 20% from its late 2022 peak. d Across the EU, ju - nior tech positions fell 35% during 2024.c The reasoning seems straightforward: If AI can generate code, why hire entry-level engineers? bS. Willison, quoted in “Vibe coding,” Wikipedia. [Online]. Available: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ Vibe_coding cAI is wiping out entry-level tech jobs, leaving graduates stranded,” Rest of World, Dec. 19, 2025. [Online]. Available: https://restofworld.org/2025/ engineering-graduates-ai-job-losses/ dAI vs Gen Z: How AI has changed the career pathway for junior developers,” Stack Overflow Blog, Dec. 26, 2025. [Online]. Available: https://stackoverflow. blog/2025/12/26/ai-vs-gen-z/ But this fundamentally misun - derstands what junior roles accom - plish. Junior engineers aren’t just cheap labor—they are the pipeline through which the industry devel - ops its future senior engineers, ar - chitects, and technical leaders. The very people this article argues are essential at every step of AI-assisted development. Less discussed but equally dam - aging is the pressure on experienced engineers. Across the industry, sea - soned developers are being man - aged out, driven by assumptions that veterans can’t adapt to AI workflows—or simply that they cost too much. This is particularly acute in some regions where negoti - ated workforce reductions dispro - portionately target older workers. Yet the engineers with the deepest architectural knowledge and most refined judgment are precisely the people best positioned to serve as the human-in-the-loop that effective AIassisted development requires. There’s also an uncomfortable economic dynamic accelerating these decisions. Companies have made massive capital investments in AI infrastructure. Those invest - ments create enormous pressure to demonstrate return on investment— and the fastest line item to cut is headcount. Organizations reduce engineering staff not because AI has absorbed those roles, but because the financial commitment to AI de - mands visible cost savings to justify the spend. This puts the cart before the horse. The benefits of AI-assisted de - velopment are real, but they depend on having skilled engineers to exe - cute disciplined workflows. Cutting the workforce to fund AI investment undermines the conditions needed for that investment to pay off.

pages.text: 114 IEEE SOFTWARE | WWW.COMPUTER.ORG/SOFTWARE | @IEEESOFTWARE SOUNDING BOARD Developing Engineers in an AI World For organizations still investing in talent development, there’s a real pedagogical question. If AI han - dles most code generation, how do new engineers develop deep techni - cal skills? There is a meaningful difference between someone who has spent years writing code—wrestling with memory management, debugging concurrency issues, tracing data through complex call stacks—and someone who has primarily reviewed AI-generated output. The former de - velops an internalized model of how software works. The latter risks a superficial understanding that col - lapses when confronted with novel failure modes. The answer isn’t to reject AI tools. It’s to be intentional. Struc - ture early-career work so juniors still write code by hand for critical learning exercises—because writ - ing, failing, debugging, and rewrit - ing is how engineering intuition is forged. Require them to review and critique AI-generated code. Pair them with seniors during architec - tural phases. Think of it as pilot training. Modern aviation uses extensive au - tomation, but no airline certifies a pilot who has never hand-flown an aircraft. Software engineering needs the same philosophy: Let AI handle routine generation, but ensure hu - mans have earned expertise through hands-on practice. The productive response isn’t eliminating roles—it’s redesign - ing them. Juniors should spend less time on mechanical code produc - tion and more on systems thinking, architecture evaluation, and critical review of AI output. Seniors should be valued explicitly for the judgment and oversight capabilities that make AI-assisted workflows reliable. Getting It Right This brings us back to where we started. The vibe coding critique is valid: Undisciplined AI-assisted development produces technical debt. But the response shouldn’t be to abandon AI—it should be to ap - ply the engineering discipline that has always been required for qual - ity software. Broy and Selic ´ recently argued in this publication that software engi - neering is exceptionally susceptible to hype, and that the generative AI wave risks drawing attention away from foundational engineering prin - ciples.2 I would argue something related but distinct: Generative AI, properly applied, reinforces those principles rather than replacing them. The teams succeeding with AI are the ones doing more systems engineering, more decomposition, more incremental verification—not less. Meanwhile, Borg, Bjarnason, and Hedin 1 have shown that vibe coding, properly scoped as a proto - typing practice, can deliver genuine value—lowering the threshold for high-fidelity prototypes that sup - port communication, validation, and exploration. The key distinction is purpose: prototyping to learn ver - sus building to ship. The engineering discipline this article advocates isn’t about rejecting rapid experimenta - tion; it’s about knowing when ex - perimentation ends and production engineering begins. T he companies that get this right will have a decisive ad - vantage. The companies that treat AI as justification to hollow out their engineering organizations will find themselves staffed by people who can prompt an LLM but can’t diagnose why the system it built is failing in production. And they will discover—too late—that they auto - mated away the one capability they couldn’t afford to lose. The AI isn’t the problem. The en - gineering is. It always has been. References 1. M. Borg, E. Bjarnason, and F. Hedin, “Vibe coding and the new prototyp - ing playbook,” IEEE Softw. , vol. 42, no. 6, pp. 12–16, Nov./Dec. 2025, doi: 10.1109/MS.2025.3597032 . 2. M. Broy and B. Selic ´, “The effects of hype in the software domain: Causes, consequences, and mitiga - tions,” IEEE Softw. , vol. 42, no. 2, pp. 98–102, Mar./Apr. 2025, doi: 10.1109/MS.2024.3511732.
